findings.trigger: Process A calls next() returning N+1 while process B calls value() concurrently; B can observe N (a value lower than the last one already issued) because the read is unlocked.
findings.recommendation: Acquire the same flock around the read in value() if a consistent snapshot against concurrent next() is required, or document that value() is a stale/optimistic read.

findings.title: The at-exactly-TTL expiry rule the module docstring promises has no test
findings.evidence: The docstring states a session is valid only while elapsed time is strictly less than the TTL and at exactly the TTL it is expired; the implementation encodes that with 'if self._clock() >= expires_at'. No test file is added and no test run was reported, so this single-character contract is unguarded.
findings.trigger: No test exercises clock() == created_at + ttl, so a future change of '>=' to '>' at line 33 (or of the matching sweep comparison) would silently extend every session by one tick and the suite would still pass.
findings.recommendation: Add tests using an injected fake clock covering: elapsed just below TTL (live, returns user), elapsed exactly TTL (None and entry removed), elapsed above TTL, unknown id (None), create-on-existing-id resetting the expiry, and sweep returning the exact count removed.

findings.title: __len__ reports stored entries, not live sessions, so it disagrees with get()
findings.evidence: __len__ returns the raw dict size; entries only disappear when get() lazily removes them or sweep() runs, so expired-but-unswept sessions still count.
findings.trigger: With a fake clock: create('a', 'u') at t=0 with ttl=10, advance the clock to t=10, then len(store) still returns 1 while store.get('a') returns None; a caller using len() as a live-session gauge reports a session that the contract says is expired.
findings.recommendation: Either document on __len__ that it is the number of retained entries (including expired ones not yet swept), or compute the live count by comparing each entry's expiry against self._clock().

findings.title: get() does a non-atomic check-then-delete; concurrent get on the same expired id raises KeyError
findings.evidence: The read of the entry and the removal are two separate dict operations with no guard: 'item = self._sessions.get(session_id)' followed later by 'del self._sessions[session_id]'. Nothing in the class serialises them.
findings.trigger: Two threads share one SessionStore and both call get(sid) for the same session after its TTL has elapsed: both execute line 29 and both take the expired branch at line 33; the first del removes the key, the second del raises an uncaught KeyError back to the caller. The same window exists between get() and sweep() on the same id.
findings.recommendation: Use 'self._sessions.pop(session_id, None)' in the expired branch (and 'self._sessions.pop(sid, None)' in sweep) so a concurrent or already-performed removal cannot raise KeyError. If the store is meant to be shared, document that it is not thread-safe or add a lock around create/get/sweep.

findings.title: ttl_seconds is converted but never validated
findings.evidence: float() accepts 0, negative, inf and nan; a zero or negative TTL creates entries that can never be live, and nan makes every comparison false so such a session never expires by get() while sweep() also never removes it.
findings.recommendation: Reject non-finite or non-positive TTLs at construction (raise ValueError) so a misconfigured TTL fails loudly instead of producing permanently-immortal or always-expired sessions.

findings.evidence: State is loaded from JSON and then indexed directly by caller-supplied upload_id, but save uses key sorting. unverified_majors.title: Authority is only terminated on /?#, so a backslash makes the parsed host disagree with WHATWG
unverified_majors.evidence: The netloc truncation loop uses only the forward-slash/query/fragment delimiters: '            netloc = netloc.split(delim, 1)[0]'. WHATWG special-scheme parsing treats a backslash as an authority terminator, which the module docstring explicitly says the split must agree with.
unverified_majors.trigger: split_url('http://evil.example\\@allowed.example/') returns host 'allowed.example' because rsplit('@', 1)[-1] keeps everything after the backslash, while a WHATWG parser stops the authority at the backslash and navigates to host 'evil.example'; a host allowlist built on this split therefore permits a request to the attacker host.
unverified_majors.recommendation: Include the backslash in the delimiter set for special schemes (or reject any netloc containing a backslash), e.g. iterate over '/?#\\' or fail closed on backslash, and add a regression test for 'http://evil.example\\@allowed.example/'.
